record.name_original: សាធារណរដ្ឋប្រជាមានិតកម្ពុជា
record.date_justification: Start 1979: after Vietnamese forces captured Phnom Penh on 7 January 1979 and routed the Khmer Rouge army, the Kampuchean People's Revolutionary Council proclaimed the new state on 8 January 1979; the official name "People's Republic of Kampuchea" (សាធារណរដ្ឋប្រជាមានិតកម្ពុជា) was adopted on 10 January 1979. End 1989: at the National Assembly session of 29-30 April 1989, presided over by Hun Sen, the PRK adopted a revised constitution (dated 30 April 1989) that renamed the state "State of Cambodia" (រដ្ឋកម្ពុជា), effective May 1989; this coincided with the withdrawal of Vietnamese occupation troops completed in September 1989. The 1979-1989 span reflects the period under the PRK name, per the Cambodian state chain (successor of Democratic Kampuchea). Wikidata Q867778 records dissolution as far as 1992 (transition to UNTAC), but the constitutional rename of April/May 1989 is the event-anchored end of the PRK as such.
record.ethical_notes: The PRK was installed by the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, whose army (up to ~200,000 troops) invaded in December 1978-January 1979 and militarily occupied Cambodia until September 1989; the PRK was a satellite/client state and its founding front (FUNSK) and leadership (Heng Samrin, Hun Sen) governed under Vietnamese and Soviet-bloc tutelage — this is occupation and imposed government, not to be euphemized. Its predecessor, Pol Pot's Democratic Kampuchea (Khmer Rouge), perpetrated the Cambodian genocide in which an estimated 1.5-2 million people (c. 20-25% of the 1975 population) died from execution, starvation, forced labour and disease (Kiernan; Heuveline). Vietnamese advisers, notably Lê Đức Thọ, controlled internal politics: first PM Pen Sovan was arrested in December 1981 (Hun Sen has said he carried out the arrest) and imprisoned in Hanoi for a decade for resisting Vietnamese dominance and demanding troop withdrawal. Historiographies conflict on framing: Vietnam and the PRK cast the intervention as liberation from genocide, while the ousted DK regime retained the UN seat with backing from China, the US and ASEAN, who condemned the occupation — AtlasPI records both readings without arbitrating.

territory_changes.description: Following Vietnam's invasion (launched 25 December 1978) and the capture of Phnom Penh on 7 January 1979, the Vietnamese-backed Kampuchean People's Revolutionary Council proclaimed the People's Republic of Kampuchea on 8 January 1979 (name formalized 10 January), replacing Pol Pot's Democratic Kampuchea; Heng Samrin became head of state.

The Vietnamese army (peaking at roughly 150,000-200,000 troops) occupied the country to sustain the PRK against Khmer Rouge and non-communist resistance based near the Thai border; the ousted Khmer Rouge retained Cambodia's UN seat with Chinese, US and ASEAN support.

At the National Assembly session of 29-30 April 1989 chaired by Hun Sen, the PRK adopted a revised constitution renaming the state the State of Cambodia (rដ្ឋកម្ពុជា) and reintroducing market-oriented reforms; Vietnam completed its troop withdrawal by September 1989, ending the PRK period.

record.name_original: រដ្ឋកម្ពុជា
record.date_justification: Start 1989: the pro-Hanoi People's Republic of Kampuchea (PRK) was reconstituted as the State of Cambodia (SOC) when its National Assembly, under Prime Minister Hun Sen, adopted an amended constitution on 29-30 April 1989 (Wikidata records the inception as 1 May 1989), renaming the polity, restoring Buddhism as state religion, reintroducing the blue field in the flag, abolishing capital punishment, and renaming the ruling Kampuchean People's Revolutionary Party to the Cambodian People's Party. End 1993: the SOC was dissolved on 24 September 1993 when the new constitution was promulgated and the monarchy restored as the Kingdom of Cambodia, following the 23 October 1991 Paris Peace Agreements, the UNTAC transitional administration (1992-1993), and the UN-supervised elections of May 1993. Vietnamese occupation forces had completed their withdrawal in September 1989, which triggered the rebranding.
record.ethical_notes: La ridenominazione da PRK a "Stato di Cambogia" nel 1989 fu una manovra di legittimazione del governo di Hun Sen e del Partito del Popolo Cambogiano (ex-KPRP), installato da Hanoi dopo l'invasione vietnamita del 1978-79 che rovesciò il regime genocida dei Khmer rossi di Pol Pot (responsabile di circa 1,5-2 milioni di morti, 1975-79). Lo Stato di Cambogia restò privo di riconoscimento internazionale: il seggio ONU restò assegnato al Governo di coalizione della Kampuchea Democratica (comprendente gli stessi Khmer rossi), sostenuto da Cina, USA e ASEAN in funzione anti-vietnamita — una scelta geopolitica che di fatto legittimò i responsabili del genocidio. Le storiografie divergono sulla natura del periodo: una lettura enfatizza la stabilizzazione e la fine dell'occupazione vietnamita, un'altra sottolinea che l'occupazione stessa aveva posto fine al genocidio Khmer rosso; entrambe le letture sono registrate senza arbitrarle.

territory_changes.description: The People's Republic of Kampuchea, the Vietnam-installed government under PM Hun Sen and the KPRP, reconstituted itself as the State of Cambodia via constitutional amendment (29-30 April 1989): Buddhism restored as state religion, capital punishment abolished, blue reintroduced to the flag, KPRP renamed Cambodian People's Party. The change coincided with the completed withdrawal of Vietnamese occupation forces in September 1989.

The Paris Peace Agreements (23 October 1991) placed the State of Cambodia and the three rival factions (FUNCINPEC, KPNLF, and the Khmer Rouge/PDK) under a Supreme National Council chaired by Norodom Sihanouk, ceding effective governance to the UN Transitional Authority in Cambodia (UNTAC). The SOC administration under Hun Sen retained control of most territory and machinery of state.

Following UN-supervised elections (May 1993) and promulgation of a new constitution, the State of Cambodia was dissolved and the monarchy restored as the Kingdom of Cambodia on 24 September 1993 under King Norodom Sihanouk, with Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen as co-prime ministers.

record.date_justification: Founded 27 April 1992 when the Assembly adopted the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, proclaiming a two-republic federation of Serbia and Montenegro as the rump/successor of the dissolving SFR Yugoslavia. End anchored to 4 February 2003, when the Federal Assembly promulgated the Constitutional Charter of Serbia and Montenegro, formally abolishing the "Federal Republic of Yugoslavia" name and converting the state into the looser State Union of Serbia and Montenegro (which itself dissolved on 3–5 June 2006 with Montenegro's independence). This record covers the FRY-named period 1992–2003; the 2003–2006 State Union is a distinct downstream phase of the same Wikidata item (Q37024).
record.ethical_notes: Il regime di Slobodan Milošević a Belgrado orchestrò la pulizia etnica in Bosnia e, nel 1998-99, in Kosovo: forze militari e di polizia serbe/jugoslave espulsero con la forza circa 863.000 albanesi del Kosovo tra marzo e giugno 1999 e ne uccisero migliaia (l'ICTY incriminò Milošević per crimini di guerra e contro l'umanità). Vanno però registrate entrambe le storiografie senza arbitrarle: i bombardamenti NATO dell'operazione Allied Force (24 marzo–9 giugno 1999), condotti senza mandato del Consiglio di Sicurezza ONU, uccisero secondo Human Rights Watch circa 500 civili (la FRY dichiarò 1.200–5.700), e la questione della legittimità dell'intervento e dello status del Kosovo resta contesa. Sul versante opposto, l'UÇK (Esercito di Liberazione del Kosovo) commise a sua volta rappresaglie e sfollamenti di serbi e rom. Le cifre demografiche qui riportate sono attribuite alle fonti (HRW, studio Lancet, censimento FRY 1991) e non vanno presentate come definitive.

territory_changes.description: On 27 April 1992 the Assembly in Belgrade adopted the FRY constitution, constituting a two-republic federation (Serbia incl. the autonomous provinces of Kosovo and Vojvodina, plus Montenegro) as the self-declared continuation of SFR Yugoslavia. The UN Security Council (Res. 777/1992) rejected automatic continuity and required reapplication for membership.

UN Security Council Resolution 757 (30 May 1992) imposed a near-total trade embargo, financial and air-traffic sanctions on the FRY for Belgrade's role in arming and directing Bosnian Serb forces during the Bosnian War; sanctions crippled the economy through the 1990s.

During the Kosovo War, Yugoslav/Serbian forces under Milošević forcibly expelled roughly 863,000 Kosovo Albanians (Mar–Jun 1999); NATO's Operation Allied Force bombed the FRY 24 Mar–9 Jun 1999, after which UNSC Res. 1244 placed Kosovo under UN administration (UNMIK/KFOR), removing it from effective Belgrade control.

On 4 February 2003 the Federal Assembly promulgated the Constitutional Charter, abolishing the name 'Federal Republic of Yugoslavia' and reconstituting the polity as the looser State Union of Serbia and Montenegro, ending the Yugoslav state name after 74 years.

sources.citation: International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY), "What is the former Yugoslavia?" — official background on the SFRY/FRY and the wars of the 1990s.
United Nations Security Council Resolution 757 (S/RES/757, 30 May 1992), imposing comprehensive sanctions on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro).
Human Rights Watch, "Under Orders: War Crimes in Kosovo" (2001) — documentation of forced expulsions and killings by Serbian/Yugoslav forces and of civilian deaths from NATO bombing.
Spiegel PB & Salama P, "War and mortality in Kosovo, 1998–99: an epidemiological testimony," The Lancet 355 (2000): 2204–2209 — CDC-linked mortality estimate (~12,000 war-related deaths).

Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Yugoslavia (former federated nation, 1929–2003)" and "Serbia and Montenegro" — standard reference for the 27 April 1992 founding, 4 February 2003 renaming, and Belgrade capital.

record.name_original: Државна заједница Србија и Црна Гора
record.date_justification: Start: the Constitutional Charter (Уставна повеља) was adopted by the Federal Assembly of the FRY and came into force on 4 February 2003, transforming the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia into the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro (Државна заједница Србија и Црна Гора), retiring the name 'Yugoslavia' after 74 years. The Charter followed the Belgrade Agreement (Accord on Principles) signed by the Serbian, Montenegrin and FRY governments in March 2002. End: Montenegro's independence referendum of 21 May 2006 passed with 55.5% for independence, just above the 55% threshold set by the EU/Venice Commission; Montenegro's parliament declared independence on 3 June 2006 and Serbia's parliament declared Serbia the legal successor to the State Union on 5 June 2006, dissolving the union. Wikidata records the dissolution as 4/June 2006.
record.ethical_notes: Il quesito dell'unione tra Serbia e Montenegro ammette due letture storiografiche che il record non arbitra (ETHICS-003). Lettura pro-indipendenza: l'unione statale del 2003 fu un contenitore lasco mediato dall'Occidente (in particolare dall'inviato UE Javier Solana, da cui il soprannome 'Solania') per rinviare la separazione, e il referendum del 21 maggio 2006 completò l'autodeterminazione montenegrina. Lettura pro-unionista/serba: la soglia del 55% fissata dall'UE fu imposta dall'esterno e l'esito (55,5%) fu talmente stretto da restare contestato. Entrambe vanno registrate con attribuzione. Va inoltre esplicitato che durante tutta l'esistenza dell'unione il Kosovo restò de iure parte della Serbia ma sotto amministrazione ONU (UNMIK) in base alla Risoluzione 1244 del Consiglio di Sicurezza (1999), conseguenza dei bombardamenti NATO e del conflitto del 1998-99; questo status irrisolto non è edulcorato ma non altera i confini nominali dell'entità.

territory_changes.description: Following the referendum of 21 May 2006 (55.5% in favour), Montenegro declared independence on 3 June 2006. On 5 June 2006 the National Assembly of Serbia declared the Republic of Serbia the legal successor of the State Union, formally dissolving Serbia and Montenegro. The separation was peaceful and referendum-based, brokered under EU mediation (Javier Solana's threshold of 55%).

Re-emergence of Serbia as a fully sovereign independent state for the first time since 1918. A new constitution — the first as an independent state since the Kingdom of Serbia's 1903 constitution — was adopted by referendum on 28-29 October 2006 and promulgated on 8 November 2006.

Kosovo's Assembly issued a unilateral declaration of independence on 17 February 2008, which Serbia rejects as illegitimate; the Serbian constitution continues to claim Kosovo and Metohija as an inalienable part of Serbia. The ICJ advisory opinion of 22 July 2010 found the declaration did not violate international law. De facto Serbian administrative control was lost after the 1998-1999 war and the NATO bombing of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Milošević era); status remains disputed.

record.date_justification: Proclaimed as the unified "Colonia Eritrea" by royal decree of King Umberto I on 1 January 1890, consolidating Italian coastal footholds established at Assab (acquired 1869-1882) and Massawa (occupied 1885). Italian rule ended de facto in 1941 during the WWII East African Campaign: after the British Commonwealth victory at the Battle of Keren (3 Feb-27 March 1941), Asmara was captured on 1 April 1941 and the Italians formally capitulated in Eritrea on 8 April 1941, after which a British Military Administration governed until 1952. (Administratively the colony had been merged into Africa Orientale Italiana in 1936, which is why some sources give 1936; but the distinct colony's existence and the end of Italian sovereignty are dated 1890-1941.)
record.ethical_notes: Colonia Eritrea was an occupation regime of the Kingdom of Italy, later intensified under Mussolini's Fascist state, which used the colony as the launchpad for the 1935-36 invasion and conquest of Ethiopia. The regime imposed racial segregation: separate "native" schools were decreed in 1909, urban segregation in Asmara in 1916, mixed marriages were banned in 1933, and "madamato" (Italian-Eritrean unions) was criminalized in 1937 with prison terms of one to five years. Italian settlers reached roughly 75,000 by 1939 (about 53,000 in Asmara alone, out of a city of ~98,000), a demographic transformation imposed on the colonized population. Eritrean troops (ascari) were also conscripted into these campaigns of conquest. The capital's Latinate name ("Eritrea," from the Greek for the Red Sea) itself supplanted indigenous designations; the highland Tigrinya kingdom of Medri Bahri is recorded as name variant and predecessor rather than erased.

territory_changes.description: King Umberto I of Italy proclaimed the unified Colony of Eritrea on 1 January 1890 by royal decree, consolidating footholds seized at Assab and Massawa (occupied 1885) under General Oreste Baratieri's occupation of the highlands.

Italian expansion inland was halted when Emperor Menelik II's Ethiopian army decisively defeated General Oreste Baratieri's Italian colonial force at the Battle of Adwa on 1 March 1896; over 7,000 Italian-side troops were killed, fixing Eritrea's southern boundary at the Mareb river.

After Mussolini's Fascist Italy invaded and conquered Ethiopia (1935-36) using Eritrea as its base, Eritrea was administratively merged into Africa Orientale Italiana (Italian East Africa) as its northern governorate.

British and Commonwealth forces defeated the Italians at the Battle of Keren (Feb-March 1941), captured Asmara on 1 April 1941, and took the Italian surrender on 8 April 1941, ending Italian rule and beginning a British Military Administration.

record.date_justification: 1069 BCE is the conventional Egyptological start (Kitchen chronology, matching Wikidata Q212728), anchored to the accession of Smendes I at Tanis and the end of the New Kingdom's 20th Dynasty on the death of Ramesses XI; some scholars date Ramesses XI's death to ~1077 BCE, so the start floats c. 1077-1069 BCE. The end, 664 BCE, is the near-universally accepted anchor: the accession of Psamtik I (Psamtek I) founding the Saite 26th Dynasty, following the Assyrian sack of Thebes and Memphis under Ashurbanipal (664 BCE) and the expulsion of the Kushite Tantamani. "Third Intermediate Period" is an Egyptological convention (originating with the German "Dritte Zwischenzeit"), not an ancient self-designation; the ancient Egyptian name for the land itself was tꜣ.wy (Tawy, "The Two Lands").
record.ethical_notes: Modelling five dynasties (21st-25th) spanning ~400 years of politically fragmented Egypt as ONE entity is a periodization simplification: for most of the period Egypt was NOT unified but split between Tanis (Lower Egypt) and the Theban High Priests of Amun (Upper Egypt), later subdivided among competing Libyan-descended (Meshwesh) rulers of the 22nd-24th dynasties. A single "capital" (Tanis) is therefore a convenience that erases contemporaneous rival seats (Thebes, Bubastis, Herakleopolis, Sais, Napata). ETHICS-002: the Kushite (Nubian) 25th Dynasty of Piye, Shabaka and Taharqa, ruling from Napata, is not a "foreign invasion" to be euphemized as decline — it reversed the earlier New Kingdom Egyptian military conquest and colonial domination of Kush (Nubia), so the "invaders" framing common in older Western Egyptology reflects the perspective of the conquered northern elite, not a neutral fact. The period ended through violence by named perpetrators: the Neo-Assyrian empire under Ashurbanipal sacked Thebes in 664 BCE and installed Psamtik I; historiographies conflict on whether the Saite 26th Dynasty represents indigenous "reunification" or an Assyrian client-state that only later won independence — both readings are recorded here without arbitration.

territory_changes.description: Accession of Smendes I at Tanis after the death of Ramesses XI ends the New Kingdom's 20th Dynasty; central authority fractures between Tanis (Lower Egypt) and the Theban High Priests of Amun (Upper Egypt), inaugurating the Third Intermediate Period.

Sheshonq I, a ruler of Libyan (Meshwesh) descent from Bubastis, founds the 22nd Dynasty and briefly re-establishes direct control over most of Egypt, before renewed fragmentation into the 23rd and 24th dynasties.

The Kushite (Nubian) king Piye (Piankhi) of Napata campaigns north and subdues the Delta rulers, uniting Egypt under the 25th Dynasty; this reverses the earlier New Kingdom Egyptian conquest and domination of Kush. Date c.728 BCE per Piye's Victory Stela; Kushite control over Upper Egypt began earlier under Kashta.

The Neo-Assyrian empire under Ashurbanipal sacks Thebes and expels the Kushite Tantamani; Psamtik I is installed at Sais and founds the Saite 26th Dynasty, ending the Third Intermediate Period and later reunifying Egypt independently.

record.date_justification: Start -664 BCE: reunification of Egypt under Psamtik I (Psamtik I) of the 26th (Saite) Dynasty, after he threw off Neo-Assyrian suzerainty and ended the Nubian 25th Dynasty's control, conventionally taken as the opening of the Late Period. End -332 BCE: Alexander III of Macedon entered Egypt and took it from the Achaemenid satrap Mazaces without a battle, ending the Second Persian Period (31st Dynasty) and the Late Period; the subsequent Argead/Ptolemaic phase is treated as a separate era. Both anchors are standard in Egyptological chronology (Metropolitan Museum: "Egypt in the Late Period, ca. 664-332 B.C."; Wikidata Q621917 start 664 BCE / end 332 BCE). Internal dynastic boundaries (esp. Third Intermediate Period/Late Period cutoff and the exact regnal years) carry a normal +/- few-year uncertainty.
record.ethical_notes: The period was defined by two foreign conquests that must be named as such, not smoothed over. In 525 BCE the Achaemenid king Cambyses II defeated Psamtik III at Pelusium, sacked Memphis and imposed direct Persian rule (27th Dynasty); Greek sources (Herodotus) portray Cambyses as a desecrator of Egyptian temples and animal cults, though modern scholarship (e.g. the Udjahorresnet inscription) argues this hostile image is partly propaganda — both readings should stand. In 343 BCE Artaxerxes III reconquered Egypt by force, expelling the last native pharaoh Nectanebo II, and ancient tradition again accuses the Persians of temple violence. The Saite capital Sais was itself the seat of an Egyptianized Libyan-descended dynasty, so "native" restoration here is a matter of degree; population figures for this era are not reliably attested and are given as null rather than invented.
